nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Florida Pompano
Scientific Name: Trachinotus carolinus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Osteichthyes
	Order:		Perciformes
	Family:	Carangidae

Other Common Names: Common pompano, Atlantic pompano, sunfish, and pompano (19 47 48 255 265 312 322 538).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Highly desired due to excellent flavor and high monetary value.  Although catches are not large and are often unpredictable, the Florida pompano forms an important fishery along the South Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coasts with Florida as the leading producer.  Most fish caught in Florida occur during winter on the west coast from Monroe County to Charlotte County primarily south of Cape Romano.  Commercially harvested fish enter the market at 250 - 360 mm TL and 0.5 - 0.7 kg, and are taken mostly by trammel nets and a few by gill nets (42 48 210 214 255 312 352).

Recreational: A favorite fish among sportsmen due to its high quality as a food fish and its fighting ability on light tackle.  Usually caught by bottom fishing offshore, or by casting from shore or boat (42 48 214 255 352).

Ecological Role: A generalized carnivore feeding predominately on the bottom of surf zone habitats where it is one of the dominant fish species (17 43 47 262).

Indicator: No known data

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Coastal waters from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to southeastern Brazil.  Widely distributed but uncommon among islands of the west Indies being most abundant along continental waters.  Uncommon north of Chesapeake Bay with highest abundance occurring along the Florida coast (232 352 48 210 312).  Common in the Indian River Lagoon (848).

Within Study Area: Harvested throughout the study area, but mainly in Louisiana (327).  Apparently more common south of the Rio Grande (303).  Commercial fished for throughout the Indian River Lagoon (1272).

Mobility and Migration
Life Mode: A dominant species of surf zone habitats.  All stages are pelagic and nektonic exhibiting diurnal activity in their feeding behavior (17 47 214 480).  Juveniles and adults show schooling behavior (47 116 651).

Apparently undergo extensive migrations, but patterns of movement are not known.  Spawning apparently takes place in offshore waters in early spring to late summer in the Gulf Stream or in locations where transport of eggs and larvae are influenced by current (210 481).  Larvae move with currents and arrive in the surf zone as juveniles ca. 10 - 15 mm TL (42 43 116 214a 255 322 482 550).  Juveniles leave surf zone when 75 - 150 mm TL for deeper water and move south along coast probably in response to colder winter temperatures (42 48 210 255 352 694).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Egg/larvae: pelagic, offshore; larvae collected at 5.5 m of depth 24.2 km in offshore marine waters (206 214 352 363).

Juveniles: Optimum habitat is shallow water, low energy, marine surf zone along open beaches with gradual slopes, but have been reported on rare occasions from marshes and bays (17 43 157 255 262 265 322 352 479 480 664 694).  Taken in salinities ranging from mesohaline to euhaline, but appear to prefer polyhaline and higher salinities(42 116 213 255 265 363 664 694).  Captive specimens were found to be able to tolerate oligohaline salinities under experimental conditions (482).

Adults: Abundant around inlets and along sandy beaches of barrier islands, and around oil platforms and artificial reefs.  Tend to be more characteristic of turbid than clear waters in marine situations although collected occasionally from bay waters.  Recorded salinities of fish collected in the wild range from mesohaline to euhaline, but captive fish have been adapted to fresh water.  Found in waters somewhat deeper than juveniles with fish over 200 mm TL being collected from depths of 33 to 40 m (47 210 214 262 303 363 538).

Substrate: Typically found over sandy bottoms with little or no rooted vegetation.  Also reported from bottoms of broken shell debris, and silt and mud (43 479 480).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae: eggs in laboratory conditions developed up to middle and late gastrulation at temperatures from 23.0 - 25.0 C (214).  Hoff et al. had strip spawned eggs hatch after 24-26h at 28oC.

Juveniles/adults: juveniles taken from 10.0 - 34.9 C (42 116 214 255 264 265 550 664), and adults from 17.0 - 31.7 C (214 363).  Majority of fish collected are from a temperature range of 28.0 - 1.7 C (214).  Temperature appears to strongly affect behavior and presence of this species.  Experimental work has shown the need for stable temperatures for maximum growth with the ideal temperature being 25.0 C or above (214).  At less than 18.0 C, feeding is reduced and ceases at 13.0 C; activity is also greatly reduced at this temperature (213).  Physiological shock becomes evident at ca. 12.0 C with partial to complete kills occurring from 10.0 - 15.5 C (48 482).  All fish have an upper lethal limit of ca. 38.0 C, although small juveniles have been observed in tide pools at temperatures above 46.0 C (482).   Pompano have been reported in Indian River Lagoon cold kills which had low temperatures down to 6 C (236 997).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Egg/larvae: Eggs developed in laboratory until mid to late gastrulation at 31.2 - 37.71 ppt (214).

Juveniles: Reported salinities range from 9.3 - 36.7 ppt with a preference shown for 20 ppt and higher (42 116 213 214 255 264 265 550 664 694).  One collection from the Texas Laguna Madre reported large schools at 45 - 50 ppt (651).  Fish in laboratory conditions were able to tolerate down to 1.27 ppt (482).

Adults: occur in salinities from 32.1- 35.6 ppt and do not normally enter water less than 32 ppt, although fish in captivity were acclimated to 1.27 ppt (363 482).

nodes.title: Other
nodes.body: Collected from a D.O. range of 3.43 - 5.64 mm/l, but are adversely affected below 4 ppm with death occurring at ca. 2.5 ppm (214 482).  Experiments with pH showed physiological shock at 11.9 and 3.9 on either end of the scale, and death occurring at 12.4 and 3.7 (482)

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Eggs and milt are probably externally fertilized by broadcasting.

Spawning Strategy:  Specific spawning areas are unknown, but probably occur offshore (210 48 214a 614 206); and over an extended period of time.  Spawning may begin as early as February and peak from April to June followed by lesser spawning in summer and early fall (July_October) with year round spawning possible in the tropical Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea (255 48 262 116 214a 352 614).

Fecundity: Probably mature after one year with spawning in wild fish unlikely until second year (213 482).  At least four different egg development stages are present in adult females indicating multiple spawning (213) with an average size female containing 6_8 hundred thousand eggs (213 214a).  Hoff et al. found fecundity low in captive pompano (7,000-9,000 eggs).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: Mature unfertilized eggs are round, symmetrical, and average 0.7 mm in diameter.  Possess large yolk with a narrow perivitelline space occupying 10 - 15% of the egg volume.  One oil globule evident, and surface of egg is smooth (213 214a).  Fertilized eggs are spherical with a single, large oil globule, partially segmented yolk mass, narrow perivitelline space, and a sculptured membrane.  Average diameter of the oil globule and egg is 0.29 mm, and 0.92 mm respectively.  Egg is almost colorless and has an irregularly segmented light yellow yolk.  The oil globule is nearly spherical and is dark yellow in a position at the top of the egg.  No chromatophore present (b).  Eggs incubated at 0 C under laboratory conditions reached blastula stage in 10 - 12 h after fertilization; mid to late gastrulation required 20 - 22 h.  Eggs nonviable after this point (b).

Larvae: No known information

Juvenile: About 7.0 mm SL and larger.  At 7.0 mm SL dorsal and anal spines prominent and soft rays evident. At 7.2 mm SL preopercular margin with 3 large spines at angle, plus 2 secondary spines on lower limb and 1 secondary spine on upper limb.  Anal fin first evident at ca. 11.0 mm SL, marginal angle spines well developed.  At 150 mm SL, all but dentary teeth disappear; by ca. 170 mm SL dentary teeth not evident (210).  Daily growth rates range from 0.5 mm/da for fish in the surf zone to 1.3 mm/da for tank reared specimens (42 363).  Rates of 25 - 42 mm for monthly growth under optimal conditions has been noted with 255 - 356 mm TL possible for first year growth (42 213 214a 482).  A weight gain of 18 g/mo was reported for captive fish and weights of 454 - 567 g were considered possible as first year weight for fish in mariculture (213 b).

Adult: Wild fish probably first spawn in second year, but in culture it may be possible to spawn them in less than 2 years (213 482).  Ripe fish taken in Florida were 275 - 380 mm Tl and weighed 456 - 1140 g (213). nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Generalized carnivores feeding primarily during the day on infaunal bottom bivalves (17 43 47 214a).  Smaller length classes are opportunistic, apparently feeding on those organisms that are most available at the time utilizing the surf to help uncover food.  Larger fish appear more selective in their diet (43).  Smallest size classes feed primarily on benthic and pelagic invertebrates frequently eating polychaetes, amphipods, gastropod larvae, insects, and some calanoid copepods.  Frequency of these decrease with size (43 48 312).  Fish 10 - 25 mm TL were found to have eaten polychaetes, amphipods, gastropod larvae, mysids, brachuran megalops, and dipteran larvae. Fish 76 - 125 mm TL fed most frequently on small clams especially Donax variablis and Hippa sp.  Larger juveniles have also been reported to feed on crab larvae, barnacles, cumacea, and fish eggs and larvae (43 48 210 214a 451 664). nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Several parasites have been reported for this species including: Protozoa - Myxobolis sp.; Nematoda Ascaris, encysted in the viscera or in the body cavity; Cestoda - Rhynchobothrium sp. encysted in mesentary and on viscera, and Scolex polymorphus; Trematoda - Aspidogaster ringens, Distonum monticelli, D. pectinatum, D. valde_inflatum, D. vitellosum, D. sp., and Monostomum sp.; Isopoda - Ione and Aegathoa in the mouth and gill area, and various body parts and fins; Copepoda - Argulus sp. on the skin (413 213).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Florida pompano (Trachinotus carolinus)

FLELMR Code: 1644

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name: Florida Pompano
Scientific Name: Trachinotus carolinus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Osteichthyes
	Order:		Perciformes
	Family:	Carangidae

Other Common Names: Common pompano, Atlantic pompano, sunfish, and pompano (19 47 48 255 265 312 322 538).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Highly desired due to excellent flavor and high monetary value.  Although catches are not large and are often unpredictable, the Florida pompano forms an important fishery along the South Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coasts with Florida as the leading producer.  Most fish caught in Florida occur during winter on the west coast from Monroe County to Charlotte County primarily south of Cape Romano.  Commercially harvested fish enter the market at 250 - 360 mm TL and 0.5 - 0.7 kg, and are taken mostly by trammel nets and a few by gill nets (42 48 210 214 255 312 352).

Recreational: A favorite fish among sportsmen due to its high quality as a food fish and its fighting ability on light tackle.  Usually caught by bottom fishing offshore, or by casting from shore or boat (42 48 214 255 352).

Ecological Role: A generalized carnivore feeding predominately on the bottom of surf zone habitats where it is one of the dominant fish species (17 43 47 262).

Indicator: No known data

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Coastal waters from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to southeastern Brazil.  Widely distributed but uncommon among islands of the west Indies being most abundant along continental waters.  Uncommon north of Chesapeake Bay with highest abundance occurring along the Florida coast (232 352 48 210 312).  Common in the Indian River Lagoon (848).

Within Study Area: Harvested throughout the study area, but mainly in Louisiana (327).  Apparently more common south of the Rio Grande (303).  Commercial fished for throughout the Indian River Lagoon (1272).

Mobility and Migration
Life Mode: A dominant species of surf zone habitats.  All stages are pelagic and nektonic exhibiting diurnal activity in their feeding behavior (17 47 214 480).  Juveniles and adults show schooling behavior (47 116 651).

Apparently undergo extensive migrations, but patterns of movement are not known.  Spawning apparently takes place in offshore waters in early spring to late summer in the Gulf Stream or in locations where transport of eggs and larvae are influenced by current (210 481).  Larvae move with currents and arrive in the surf zone as juveniles ca. 10 - 15 mm TL (42 43 116 214a 255 322 482 550).  Juveniles leave surf zone when 75 - 150 mm TL for deeper water and move south along coast probably in response to colder winter temperatures (42 48 210 255 352 694).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Egg/larvae: pelagic, offshore; larvae collected at 5.5 m of depth 24.2 km in offshore marine waters (206 214 352 363).

Juveniles: Optimum habitat is shallow water, low energy, marine surf zone along open beaches with gradual slopes, but have been reported on rare occasions from marshes and bays (17 43 157 255 262 265 322 352 479 480 664 694).  Taken in salinities ranging from mesohaline to euhaline, but appear to prefer polyhaline and higher salinities(42 116 213 255 265 363 664 694).  Captive specimens were found to be able to tolerate oligohaline salinities under experimental conditions (482).

Adults: Abundant around inlets and along sandy beaches of barrier islands, and around oil platforms and artificial reefs.  Tend to be more characteristic of turbid than clear waters in marine situations although collected occasionally from bay waters.  Recorded salinities of fish collected in the wild range from mesohaline to euhaline, but captive fish have been adapted to fresh water.  Found in waters somewhat deeper than juveniles with fish over 200 mm TL being collected from depths of 33 to 40 m (47 210 214 262 303 363 538).

Substrate: Typically found over sandy bottoms with little or no rooted vegetation.  Also reported from bottoms of broken shell debris, and silt and mud (43 479 480).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Eggs/larvae: eggs in laboratory conditions developed up to middle and late gastrulation at temperatures from 23.0 - 25.0 C (214).  Hoff et al. had strip spawned eggs hatch after 24-26h at 28oC.

Juveniles/adults: juveniles taken from 10.0 - 34.9 C (42 116 214 255 264 265 550 664), and adults from 17.0 - 31.7 C (214 363).  Majority of fish collected are from a temperature range of 28.0 - 1.7 C (214).  Temperature appears to strongly affect behavior and presence of this species.  Experimental work has shown the need for stable temperatures for maximum growth with the ideal temperature being 25.0 C or above (214).  At less than 18.0 C, feeding is reduced and ceases at 13.0 C; activity is also greatly reduced at this temperature (213).  Physiological shock becomes evident at ca. 12.0 C with partial to complete kills occurring from 10.0 - 15.5 C (48 482).  All fish have an upper lethal limit of ca. 38.0 C, although small juveniles have been observed in tide pools at temperatures above 46.0 C (482).   Pompano have been reported in Indian River Lagoon cold kills which had low temperatures down to 6 C (236 997).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Egg/larvae: Eggs developed in laboratory until mid to late gastrulation at 31.2 - 37.71 ppt (214).

Juveniles: Reported salinities range from 9.3 - 36.7 ppt with a preference shown for 20 ppt and higher (42 116 213 214 255 264 265 550 664 694).  One collection from the Texas Laguna Madre reported large schools at 45 - 50 ppt (651).  Fish in laboratory conditions were able to tolerate down to 1.27 ppt (482).

Adults: occur in salinities from 32.1- 35.6 ppt and do not normally enter water less than 32 ppt, although fish in captivity were acclimated to 1.27 ppt (363 482).

sections.heading: Other
sections.content: Collected from a D.O. range of 3.43 - 5.64 mm/l, but are adversely affected below 4 ppm with death occurring at ca. 2.5 ppm (214 482).  Experiments with pH showed physiological shock at 11.9 and 3.9 on either end of the scale, and death occurring at 12.4 and 3.7 (482)

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  Eggs and milt are probably externally fertilized by broadcasting.

Spawning Strategy:  Specific spawning areas are unknown, but probably occur offshore (210 48 214a 614 206); and over an extended period of time.  Spawning may begin as early as February and peak from April to June followed by lesser spawning in summer and early fall (July_October) with year round spawning possible in the tropical Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea (255 48 262 116 214a 352 614).

Fecundity: Probably mature after one year with spawning in wild fish unlikely until second year (213 482).  At least four different egg development stages are present in adult females indicating multiple spawning (213) with an average size female containing 6_8 hundred thousand eggs (213 214a).  Hoff et al. found fecundity low in captive pompano (7,000-9,000 eggs).
